text: The Vallow–Daybell doomsday murders involve a series of killings, including child murder, filicide, and spousal murder, committed by Lori Vallow Daybell and Chad Daybell. The couple led a Mormon religious sect described as a "doomsday cult" with beliefs significantly deviating from mainstream LDS Church teachings. The murders began when Lori's estranged husband, Charles Vallow, was shot dead by her brother Alex Cox on July 11, 2019, in Chandler, Arizona. On September 9 and 23, 2019, Lori's daughter Tylee Ryan (16) and adopted son Joshua Jaxon "J. J." Vallow (7) disappeared from their home in Rexburg, Idaho, and their remains were found on June 9, 2020. The bodies were buried on property owned by Chad, who was Lori's lover at the time of their deaths and had become her husband by the time the bodies were discovered. On October 2, 2019, Lori's nephew-in-law Brandon Boudreaux survived a murder attempt in Gilbert, Arizona, and on October 19, 2019, Chad's wife Tammy was murdered at their home in Rexburg. Lori and Chad married two weeks after Tammy's death. After the children's disappearances, Tammy's body was exhumed and her death was ruled a homicide. On February 20, 2020, Lori was arrested for desertion and non-support of her children. On June 9, 2020, police discovered the children's remains at Chad's property, and Chad was arrested. On May 25, 2021, both were charged with first-degree murders of Tylee, J.J., and Tammy. Prosecutors stated the couple conspired with Alex Cox to commit the murders as part of their apocalyptic beliefs, to remove obstacles to their affair, and to collect life insurance and Social Security benefits, using religion to justify the crimes. Lori and Chad were tried separately; on May 12, 2023, Lori was found guilty of all charges related to the killings and sentenced to multiple consecutive life imprisonment without parole. On May 30, 2024, Chad was also found guilty of all charges and sentenced to death. After her Idaho sentencing, Lori was extradited to Arizona to stand trial twice—first for the murder of Charles Vallow and then for the attempted murder of Brandon Boudreaux—where she acted as her own attorney, causing multiple court incidents. On April 22, 2025, she was found guilty of conspiring to murder Charles Vallow, and on June 12, 2025, guilty of conspiring to murder Brandon Boudreaux, receiving two additional life sentences. Both Chad and Lori have appealed their sentences. Chad Daybell, born August 11, 1968, in Provo, Utah, grew up in Springville and attended Brigham Young University, graduating with a B.A. in journalism. He worked as a copy editor and later as a cemetery sexton, and published his first novel, An Errand for Emma, in 1999. In 2001, he published One Foot in the Grave, and in 2004, co-founded Spring Creek Book Company to self-publish books promoting apocalyptic beliefs. By the end of the 2000s, the Daybells faced financial difficulties, with Chad's publishing business generating about $2,000 annually, and both working part-time jobs. Chad gained popularity among radical Mormon "preppers" who believed the end of the world was imminent, publishing dozens of books depicting apocalyptic scenarios and featuring characters based on his family. He claimed to have had two near-death experiences that allowed him to receive supernatural visions from "beyond the veil," and often discussed these experiences on the Mormon forum "Another Voice of Warning." His religious views became increasingly extreme starting around 2006–2007, with claims of visions about earthquakes, war, and destruction in the Americas beginning in 2010 or 2011. In 2015, he claimed to have heard a voice instructing him to move to Rexburg, Idaho, and prophesied an earthquake in Utah that year. Lori Ryan Daybell, born June 26, 1973, in Loma Linda, California, grew up in a Mormon family with parents who were tax protesters and in conflict with the IRS. She married Joseph Anthony Ryan Jr. in 2001, had a daughter Tylee in 2002, and divorced him in 2005, later accusing him of sexual assault in a bitter custody battle. In 2007, her brother Alex Cox attacked Ryan, resulting in a 90-day jail sentence. In 2018, Ryan died from arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and after Lori's 2020 arrest, police reviewed the case and found no evidence of foul play. In February 2006, Lori married Charles Vallow. In 2013, the couple adopted J.J. Vallow, whose biological parents were unable to care for him due to substance abuse, and who was born with drugs in his system and diagnosed with autism. Around 2015, Lori became interested in Chad's Standing in Holy Places series. In October 2018, she met Chad at a "Preparing a People" event with Melanie Gibb and Zulema Pastenes, where she displayed flirtatious behavior. Chad and Lori began communicating privately, and after a small gathering in December 2018, they became lovers. They formed a religious group called the "Church of the Firstborn," with Chad as leader, including members such as Melani Boudreaux, Gibb, Cox, and Pastenes. The group believed in reincarnation, which is not accepted by the LDS Church, with Chad claiming to have lived 31 previous lives and Lori 21, five of which overlapped with his. They believed people were categorized as "light" or "dark" based on their affiliation with Jesus or Satan, and used a "scoring system" to assign good and evil ratings. "Dark" individuals were believed to be possessed by evil spirits, and in some cases, could become "zombies," which could only be eliminated by killing the person. Seven women, including Lori and Pastenes, called themselves the "seven gatherers" and conducted "castings" via Zoom. Chad and Lori also used a "vibration" scale, believing those with sufficient vibrations possessed special powers or could be translated. They believed in teleportation and "dark and light portals," with Chad claiming to create such portals to interact spiritually with Lori, receive revelations, and travel to other realms. Chad predicted the world would end on July 22, 2020, and claimed to be guided by angels, while Lori believed she was an "exalted goddess" with visionary powers destined to lead the 144,000 survivors. Zulema Pastenes stated Lori believed she could not be held responsible for her actions as an exalted being. Experts have categorized their beliefs as Mormon fundamentalism or "Mormon fanfic," taking LDS tenets and reinterpreting them to extreme levels. By February 2019, Lori told Charles she no longer cared about him or J.J., vanished for 58 days, and filed for divorce citing threats to his life, theft of his truck and $35,000 from their joint accounts, and claims that he was possessed by a "dark spirit" named "Ned Schneider." Lori claimed she was a god assigned to carry out the work of the 144,000 at Christ's Second Coming in July 2020 and would murder him if he interfered with her mission. Charles sought a protective order, which he later withdrew, stating he wanted to try to make the marriage work.

Chad and Lori were active in the far right fringes of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, operating within an "ecosystem of extremism" that enabled their connections.[106] By February 2019, Lori informed Charles that she no longer cared about him or their son J.J. and then vanished for 58 days.[74] That same month, Charles filed for divorce, citing threats to his life, the theft of his truck, and the unauthorized withdrawal of $35,000 from their joint bank accounts.[107] According to Charles' filing, Lori claimed he was possessed by a "dark spirit" named "Ned Schneider," that she was a "god assigned to carry out the work of the 144,000 at Christ's Second Coming," which she believed would occur in July 2020, and that she would murder him if he interfered with her mission.[108][103] Charles sought a protective order from his attorney, but withdrew the petition one month later, stating he wanted to try to make the marriage work.[54] In February 2019, he changed the beneficiary of his $1 million life insurance policy to his sister Kay, not his wife Lori, a change Lori did not learn about until after Charles' death.[109] Arizona police later retrieved text messages between Chad, Lori, and her brother Alex Cox that referred to Charles as "Ned" or "Hiplos," the names of the spirit said to possess him.[110] Lori told members of her religious group that Charles had become a "zombie," and several followers repeatedly prayed for his death.[98] After discovering Lori's affair with Chad Daybell, Charles confronted her and, eleven days before his death, sent an email to Tammy Daybell informing her that their spouses were cheating.[98] Evidence showed Tammy had opened and deleted the message and blocked Charles' email address.[111] On July 1, 2019, Charles told Lori he planned to meet Tammy in person, and at that time, Lori and Chad were communicating constantly using burner phones.[112] On July 11, 2019, Charles went to pick up J.J. at Lori's home in Chandler, Arizona, with Alex Cox present; an altercation occurred and Cox shot and killed Charles.[6][113][114] Tylee reported that she grabbed a baseball bat after hearing Charles, Lori, and Cox arguing, that Charles took the bat from her, and that she ran away with J.J. before the shooting.[115] Cox claimed self-defense, asserting he retrieved his gun after Charles struck him on the head with the bat.[101][116] Lori did not call 911; it was later determined that Alex Cox called it about 45 minutes after Charles was killed.[117] Moments after the shooting, Lori took J.J. to school and stopped at Burger King and Walgreens to buy flip-flops.[118] No charges were pressed.[101][119] A detective testified that Lori's behavior that day was oddly "nonchalant" and that she seemed unaffected.[120] Zulema Pastenes stated that Cox told her he did not feel bad because he had killed a "zombie."[82] Investigations revealed that two days before the shooting, Lori sent her brother a text saying to "be like Nephi," which police interpreted as a command to kill a wicked man.[117] Lori texted Charles' sons from a previous marriage that their father had "passed away," then left them without further information for three days.[121][122] The sons had to find the mortuary where their father's body was and organize a memorial service, which Lori did not attend.[121] Before his death, Charles' attorneys noted he was primarily concerned for J.J.'s safety and well-being, as the boy had special needs requiring a consistent routine, and he was also concerned for Tylee, though he could not legally include her in the divorce filings because she was not his biological daughter and he had not adopted her.[54] Days after Charles was killed, Chad sent Lori a love story in the form of text messages, which investigators called a "romance novel," describing a sexual relationship between "James" and "Elena," names Chad used for himself and Lori.[123][124] By the end of August, Lori relocated to Rexburg, Idaho, with her children, and Alex Cox also moved there.[123] Just before moving to Idaho, Lori sold J.J.'s service dog.[126] While living in Rexburg, neighbors noticed J.J.'s erratic behavior, as Lori often left him outside without adult supervision for long periods; when confronted, Lori claimed he was "her niece's drug baby" and did not mention his autism.[76] Tylee was last seen on September 8, 2019, at Yellowstone National Park with her brother J.J., her mother Lori, and her uncle Alex Cox.[54] She was never enrolled at any school in Idaho, despite her mother claiming she was attending BYU-Idaho.[123] J.J. last attended Rexburg's Kennedy Elementary School on September 20. On September 22, Melanie Gibb and her boyfriend David Warwick were staying at Lori's home; around 10:30 p.m., Warwick saw Alex Cox take J.J., who was sleeping, upstairs to his bedroom. This was J.J.'s last confirmed sighting. The next morning, J.J. was absent; Lori told Gibb and Warwick that J.J. had been misbehaving so Alex had picked him up.[127] On September 23, J.J. had an unexcused absence from school.[128] The next day, Lori informed the school that she would now be homeschooling J.J.[129] In the months following the children's disappearances, Lori continued to collect Social Security Survivor benefits for each child after their father's death.[130] In October 2019, two Venmo payments were made from Tylee's account to her older half-brother Colby Ryan with love-expressing messages; when Colby expressed concern, he received responses indicating Tylee was safe but too busy to talk.[54] After repeated unanswered calls, Colby became more worried.[131] Brandon Boudreaux[102] and Melanie Gibb[97][132] later stated that Lori and Chad believed Tylee and J.J. were "possessed" and had become "zombies."[133] Zulema Pastenes testified that Chad told his followers that J.J. would die soon and come back as Colby's son.[82] Investigators found text messages in which Lori and Chad discussed the "possession" of Tylee and J.J. and mentioned "a perfectly orchestrated plan to take the children"; a text exchange between Lori and Alex Cox referenced "working on Z's," referring to zombies.[134] On October 2, 2019, Brandon Boudreaux, the estranged husband of Lori's niece Melani, was shot at from a Jeep while driving home in Gilbert, Arizona. The bullet missed his head by inches. Boudreaux recognized the Jeep as one used by Tylee Ryan and could provide its license plate, which was registered to Charles Vallow.[69][135] Melani had become involved in her aunt's religious activities in 2018 and had insisted on buying food stockpiles for the end of the world; during summer 2019, she demanded a divorce, which was not finalized when Boudreaux was shot at.[136] Boudreaux said he was blindsided by the divorce request, which he blamed on Melani's involvement in her aunt's "cult."[54] Boudreaux, suspecting Lori and Alex of Charles' killing, hired a private investigator.[137] After the children went missing, he believed Charles' death, the children's disappearance, and the attempt on his life were connected to Lori's religious group and suspected the murder attempt was motivated by his life insurance policy.[136] Prosecutors later stated that Lori hoped to access Boudreaux's money through her niece.[69] In February 2020, Boudreaux filed a court document claiming the attempt on his life was motivated by insurance money, that the gunman was likely Lori's recently deceased brother Alex Cox, and that Melani was likely aware of Tylee and J.J.'s whereabouts.[56][138] Melani denied any knowledge of what happened to the children.[121] By tracking Alex Cox's cell phone data, investigators found that Cox had searched online for directions to Boudreaux's address and had been near his home before the shooting.[139] He had also searched "how to load ammunition," "ballistic trajectory calculators," and, after the shooting, "man shot in Gilbert."[140] On the day of the shooting, Cox and Lori communicated several times; later, Lori also made Internet searches about a shooting in Gilbert, Arizona.[139] In February 2019, Chad told his neighbors Todd and Alice Gilbert that he had a vision that Tammy would die before her 50th birthday.[141] On October 9, 2019, Tammy reported being shot at in her driveway by a masked man with what she thought was a paintball gun; the man pulled the trigger several times, but the gun appeared unloaded. Police believed it was a prank and could not identify the man.[54] Ten days later, Tammy was found dead in her home, apparently from natural causes. Chad claimed she had retired the previous night with a terrible cough and died in her sleep.[142] He said she had low blood pressure, seizures, and negative reactions to homeopathic medicines, though no medical records supported this.[112] Tammy's funeral was held in Utah three days after her death. Alice Gilbert said she was surprised it came so soon and felt it had been "planned." The Gilberts testified that Chad did not seem devastated and acted in a "businesslike" manner.[141] Chad's sister-in-law, Heather Daybell, said Chad's behavior at the funeral did not seem genuine and that he "just didn't seem upset."[143] Jason Gwilliam said Chad was "not crying but trying to cry."[53] During the service, Chad mentioned Tammy suffered from depression, said she was not easy to live with, and called her "lazy."[144] Police reports indicate Chad received life insurance payouts after Tammy's death totaling $430,000 (equivalent to about $529,000 in 2024).[48] Tammy's body was not autopsied initially due to Chad's refusal and the coroner's acceptance of his decision. After exhumation and autopsy, it was determined she had been asphyxiated by someone else; the autopsy results, completed in February 2021, were not publicly released until April 2023 during Lori's trial.[18][54] Investigators found text messages between Chad and Lori claiming Tammy was in "limbo" and possessed by a spirit named "Viola," and at some point, they told their followers that Tammy had become a "zombie."[145] Alex Cox's phone was located near the Daybells' residence on October 9, four hours before Tammy was shot at, and pinged again in the same area ten days later, on the night Tammy died.[146][147] Police found at Cox's home an AR-15 resembling the description Tammy gave of the supposed paintball gun. Cox had searched online about the use of an AR-15 and how a Grendel round would impact a Dodge Dakota, which was the car the Daybells owned.[148] Prosecutors stated the "paintball gun" Tammy saw on October 9 was a real gun,[149] possibly jammed or misfired,[148] and the shooter was likely Alex Cox.[149] Zulema Pastenes testified that she had been with Lori and her niece Melani doing a "casting" on the night Tammy was attacked; during that time, Lori talked on the phone and became very angry, calling the person "idiot, moron, stupid," then said after hanging up, "idiot can't do anything by himself."[82] The day after Tammy's funeral, Chad introduced Lori to his children.[150] One week after Tammy's death, he told Todd and Alice Gilbert that he had found the woman he would marry. Days later, he brought Lori to meet the Gilberts. Alice described the meeting as "awkward," with Chad and Lori laughing and being affectionate, more so than with Tammy. Chad also mentioned that Lori "recently had a daughter who had passed away."[141] Chad told Tammy's sister, Samantha Gwilliam, that Tammy's spirit appeared to him at the cemetery and advised him to "move on." He also told Samantha that he and Lori had bonded over their recently dead spouses and that Lori had no children, so they would be "empty nesters."[151][152] Chad and Lori were married in Hawaii on November 5, 2019, two weeks after Tammy's death and two months after Tylee and J.J. (not yet known to be missing) were murdered.[54] Chad did not inform his family beforehand; his mother discovered the marriage upon meeting Lori.[52][143] Investigators found in Lori's internet history that she had ordered wedding rings in August 2019 and searched for wedding dresses on the day of Tammy's burial.[154] On November 26, police visited Lori's townhouse in Rexburg for a welfare check on J.J. at the request of his grandmother, Kay Woodcock. A detective initially found Chad and Alex Cox at the home; both acted suspiciously—Cox, unaware it was Kay who requested the check, claimed J.J. was with his grandmother, and Chad, known to be married to Lori, said he was a friend of Alex and "hardly knew" Lori.[155] Police later reached Lori, who claimed J.J. was in Arizona with her friend Melanie Gibb.[54] However, when contacted, Gibb stated J.J. had not been with her for several months.[156] That night, a neighbor observed Lori and Alex Cox packing a truck outside her home. The following day, when police and FBI arrived to search the house, it was abandoned. Chad's home was also searched.[157] Lori and Chad returned to Hawaii, where they resided in a gated community in Princeville on the island of Kauai,[158] living off the money Chad received from Tammy's life insurance.[48] While searching for a home in Hawaii, Chad wrote in an application that the couple had no children.[159] Prosecutors in Idaho became involved when police requested a warrant to locate the Jeep used in the shooting in Arizona.[160] On December 6, 2019, Melanie Gibb contacted police, revealing that both Lori and Chad had called her separately on November 26 and asked her to tell police that J.J. was with her.[156] Police efforts to locate J.J. led to the discovery that Tylee was also missing.[161] A connection was made between the Idaho and Arizona investigations.[160] Law enforcement intensified inquiries into the children's whereabouts and Chad and Lori's departure from Idaho, and decided to further investigate Tammy's death: her body was exhumed for an autopsy on December 11.[18][54] On December 20, the Rexburg Police Department announced the children were officially missing and asked the public to help locate them. Investigators expressed concern for their safety, asserting they were not with Chad and Lori and that Lori had refused to cooperate with the investigation, choosing to leave the state with Chad instead. Police also stated the children's disappearance could be linked to Tammy Daybell's "suspicious death." The next day, police identified Lori and Chad as "persons of interest."[54] The case received national coverage, with family and friends describing Chad and Lori's "cult-like" beliefs in interviews and social media posts.[136] On December 23, 2019, the Daybells released statements through a Rexburg attorney, who said that "Chad Daybell was a loving husband and he has the support of his children in this matter," adding that Lori was a "devoted mother" who "resents assertions to the contrary" and that the "allegations" would be addressed "once they have"

Tammy's body was exhumed for an autopsy on December 11. On December 20, the Rexburg Police Department announced that the children were officially missing and asked the public to help locate them, expressing concern that they were not with Chad and Lori, and that Lori had refused to cooperate with the investigation, opting to leave the state with Chad. Police linked the children's disappearance to Tammy Daybell's "suspicious death" and the next day identified Lori and Chad as "persons of interest." The case received national coverage, with family and friends describing Chad and Lori's "cult-like" beliefs. On December 23, 2019, the Daybells released statements through a Rexburg attorney, claiming Chad was a loving husband supported by his children and Lori was a "devoted mother" who "resents assertions to the contrary," stating the "allegations" would be addressed "once they have moved beyond speculation and rumor." Colby Ryan, J.J.'s grandparents Larry and Kay Woodcock, and Chad's brother Matt Daybell issued messages asking Lori and Chad to return the children. On January 7, 2020, the Woodcocks held a press conference in Rexburg offering a $20,000 reward for the children's return or information leading to them. On January 25, 2020, after Lori and Chad were located in Kauai, law enforcement served them with a court order requiring Lori to "physically produce" Tylee and J.J. within five days to the Idaho Department of Welfare or the Rexburg Police Department. The next day, police seized their rental car and searched their rental townhome in Princeville, where they found Tylee's debit card and J.J.'s iPad. Also on January 26, the Daybells were confronted by East Idaho News reporter Nate Eaton, who they refused to answer. In February 2020, authorities focused on a storage locker in Rexburg rented by Lori in October 2019, discovering belongings linked to Tylee and J.J., including clothing, bikes, and photographs, left behind when Lori left Rexburg in late November 2019. Video footage captured Lori and Alex Cox moving items to and from the locker before her departure. On November 24, 2019, Chad Daybell gave Alex Cox a "patriarchal blessing," which he had no standing to give in the LDS Church, saying Alex had assisted him and Lori "in ways that can never be repaid," calling him a prophet and a hero and predicting he would be a "messenger of the Lord." The recording was later found on Lori's iCloud account. Alex Cox died on December 12, 2019, attributed to blood clots and high blood pressure. The day before his death, Cox had been told by Lori and Chad that Tammy Daybell's body was going to be exhumed. Zulema Pastenes testified that Cox had told her he was worried about being Lori and Chad's "fall guy." On February 20, 2020, Lori was arrested in Hawaii by the Kauai Police Department and on March 5 was extradited back to Idaho. Lori faced charges in Madison County, Idaho, including two felony counts of desertion and nonsupport of dependent children, and three misdemeanors. Her bail was initially set at $5 million but was later lowered to $1 million after extradition. In May, Lori appeared in court to request a further reduction, which was denied. Multiple local bond companies were reportedly unwilling to work with her. After Lori's arrest, Chad returned to Idaho and tried to convince the Gilberts to put their home up for bond to get Lori out of prison, claiming Jesus had given him the idea. When Alice Gilbert asked him about the children and confronted him on what he had said about Lori's daughter being dead, Chad answered it was a custody issue and added that Tylee "didn't like people" and did not like him, using the past tense. On June 9, police found human remains buried in unmarked graves in the backyard of Chad's home during a search, with Tylee's remains in the pet cemetery area used for burying pets and J.J.'s remains in a separate area near a pond. As the property was searched, Chad phoned Lori in jail to warn her and tried to drive off after the bodies were found, but was chased down and apprehended for obstruction or concealment of evidence. His bail was set at $1 million the next day. Authorities began searching Daybell's property after tracking Alex Cox's cell phone. On September 9, 2019, the day after Tylee's last sighting, Cox's phone pinged at Lori's home, then at Daybell's home, and on September 23, the day after J.J. was last seen, it pinged again at Daybell's property. The FBI also intercepted a September 9 text between Chad and Tammy, in which Chad said he had shot a large raccoon in their backyard and buried it in their "pet cemetery," which investigators found suspicious as raccoons are normally nocturnal. On June 10, the Woodcock and Ryan families confirmed the human remains were those of Tylee and J.J. This was officially confirmed by Rexburg police three days later. Tylee's body was burned; her hands were cut off and her bones were fractured, indicating dismemberment. J.J.'s body was wrapped in plastic and buried under rocks and wooden planks. J.J. had been asphyxiated with a plastic bag and duct tape over his mouth. Tylee's cause of death could not be determined and was ruled a "homicide by unspecified means." Tylee's DNA was found on a pickaxe and shovel at Chad's home. Alex Cox's fingerprints and Lori's hair were found on the plastic and duct tape on J.J.'s remains. In August, Chad Daybell was excommunicated by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints on the basis of his religious teachings, described by the media as a "doomsday cult." On July 2, 2020, prosecutors dropped two charges against Lori related to desertion and nonsupport and instead charged her with obstruction or concealment of evidence regarding her children's remains. On July 17, her bond was lowered by Madison County judge Michelle Mallard to $50,000 per charge, totaling $150,000, with Chad still required to post $1 million in Fremont County to be released. On May 25, 2021, Chad and Lori were indicted on charges of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder for the deaths of Tylee, J.J., and Tammy, as well as grand theft by deception regarding the children. Lori was also charged with grand theft related to her children's Social Security Survivor benefits. Chad faced an insurance fraud charge related to Tammy's life insurance policy. In June 2021, Lori was indicted by a grand jury in Maricopa County, Arizona, on one count of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder for the death of Charles Vallow. Police documents stated the evidence showed Charles' death was planned to prevent him from confronting Lori about her religious beliefs and to allow Chad and Lori to marry and fulfill their religious prophecy. In July 2021, prosecutors in Maricopa County decided not to prosecute Chad in connection with Charles Vallow, citing "no reasonable likelihood of conviction." In September 2021, Chad's children issued a statement defending their father's innocence, claiming he had been "fooled in the worst, most deadly way possible" by Lori Vallow. In 2022, Lori was indicted on one count of first-degree premeditated murder related to the attempt on Brandon Boudreaux's life. A jury trial for the Madison County charges against Lori was initially set for January 25–29, 2021. On May 27, 2021, Lori was found incompetent and unfit to stand trial, and her case was stayed. In December 2021, Lori's attorney Mark Means was disqualified due to representing both Lori and Chad. On April 11, 2022, Lori was deemed competent to stand trial after mental health treatment. On October 6, 2022, after her new defense team filed motions, Judge Steven W. Boyce suspended the case until her competency could be determined. On November 16, she was found competent again. Lori and Chad both pleaded not guilty to all charges in Idaho. Their cases were split in March 2023 at Chad's request, because Chad had waived his right to a speedy trial and his attorneys needed more time to review DNA evidence, and due to the "mutually antagonistic nature of the defendants' positions." Since Lori had not waived her right to a swift trial, her case proceeded as planned. On March 21, 2023, the judge removed the death penalty from Lori due to newly uncovered DNA evidence discovered too close to trial to be tested and admitted. Lori's trial began on April 3, 2023, in the Ada County Courthouse in Boise, Idaho. She did not testify and her lawyers did not call any witnesses, while the prosecution called about 60 people. On April 15, pictures of the children's corpses were shown to jurors and audience, and Lori asked to be excused, which was denied. Melanie Gibb, Audrey Barattiero (a former friend of Lori who had participated in her religious group), and Ian Pawlowski (the husband of Lori's niece Melani) testified about Lori's beliefs and her claims of casting out Satan. Barattiero said that when she grew uncomfortable with Lori's beliefs and decided to end their friendship, Lori threatened to murder her and dispose of her body in trash bags. Prosecutors stated that Lori had "groomed" and "manipulated" her brother Alex Cox to participate in the crimes. Lori's sister Summer Shiflet testified that Alex had suffered brain damage in a car accident and that his decision-making was "stuck at a teenage level." Zulema Pastenes said Alex was entirely under the influence of Chad and Lori, who convinced him he was a reincarnated warrior of God and that "the only reason he had come to Earth was to protect Lori." During closing arguments, Lori's attorney Jim Archibald depicted her as under Chad's psychological control. Prosecutor Rob Wood summarized the evidence showing Lori's participation in the conspiracy to commit all three murders and reminded the jury that she had never reported her children were missing and had lied about their whereabouts. On May 12, 2023, Lori was found guilty of all criminal charges. On July 31, 2023, she received three consecutive life sentences without parole for the murders of Tylee, J.J., and the conspiracy to commit murder of Tammy, plus fines and restitution for the grand theft charges. Judge Boyce stated that Lori had murdered her children to "remove them as obstacles and to profit financially," choosing "the most evil and destructive path possible" to justify the killings. Before sentencing, Lori made her first public statement since arrest, saying she had been speaking to Jesus, her children, and Tammy, and that they were "happy and extremely busy" in heaven. She claimed "Jesus Christ knows that no one was murdered in this case. Accidental deaths happen, suicides happen, fatal side effects from medications happen." An alternate juror described Lori as "a monster" after seeing graphic photos of the children and the Hawaii wedding photos after the murders. On May 30, 2025, Lori's attorney filed a notice of appeal for her 2023 conviction, demanding a new trial. On November 9, 2023, Chad's legal team filed three motions to remove the death penalty in his trial, stating Lori had "manipulated" Chad through emotional and sexual control and that he had "lesser culpability" than Lori, who did not face the death penalty. The motions were denied in December. Chad's trial opened on April 10, 2024. In his opening statement, prosecutor Wood portrayed Chad as motivated by "sex, money, and power" and craving significance, seeing his spouse and Lori's children as obstacles. Chad's attorney John Prior painted him as a religious man lured into adultery by Lori, focusing on Alex Cox's history of violence and his role as "Lori's protector." On May 16, Chad's defense filed a motion for acquittal after an amended indictment incorrectly listed J.J.'s death as occurring between September 8–9, 2019, instead of September 22–23. Judge Boyce ruled the clerical error was not grounds for acquittal. Two of Chad's children, Emma and Garth, testified in his defense, saying their mother had health problems and was "getting tired extremely easily." Three former colleagues of Tammy Daybell testified that she seemed healthy and energetic up until the day before her death, and Tammy's sister testified she seemed fine when she visited on October 14, 2019. Chad did not take the stand. During closing arguments, prosecutor Lindsey Blake summarized evidence pointing to Chad's crucial role in coordinating and giving religious justification for the murders. Prior argued Lori and Alex Cox were the true culprits, stating Lori was motivated by greed, had manipulated Chad all along, and that Chad would likely have been her next victim. On May 30, 2024, the jury found Chad guilty of first-degree murder and conspiracy in the deaths of Tammy, Tylee, and J.J., as well as guilty of grand theft by deception related to the children's deaths and insurance fraud related to Tammy's life insurance. The prosecution sought the death penalty for Chad. At sentencing, Chad chose not to present any mitigation evidence. On June 1, 2024, he was sentenced to death. For the insurance fraud charges, he was sentenced to 15 years in prison, each to run concurrent to death and to restitution of $130,000 plus $300,000, with no fines added due to being deemed indigent. Tammy Daybell's extended family, Matt and Heather Daybell, as well as the Boudreaux, Cox, and Shiflet families issued statements expressing relief at the end of the Idaho trials and their thoughts for the victims. Chad was placed on death row at Idaho Maximum Security Institution. On June 5, 2024, Chad's attorneys filed a notice of appeal to the Idaho Supreme Court asking for a review of the verdict.

In November 2023, Lori was extradited to Arizona to face two conspiracy charges; she pleaded not guilty. Her trial was initially scheduled for August 1, 2024, but was postponed due to the volume of evidence, and later moved to February 24, 2025, after her defense filed a motion for delay. Lori objected and maintained her right to a speedy trial. In October 2024, Colby Ryan posted on his YouTube channel a recording of a phone call with his mother, in which Lori claimed to have received "higher knowledge" from Jesus, was on a "divine mission," stated that Tylee and J.J. had visited her in spirit, and suggested Tylee accidentally killed J.J. and then took her own life in remorse; Colby commented that his mother was "beyond deceived." Also in October 2024, Lori's attorneys requested a competency hearing, and one week later, she requested to waive her right to counsel and represent herself. On December 5, 2024, a doctor found her mentally fit and competent to stand trial, and Judge Justin Beresky granted her request to represent herself, noting she had "real trial experience" and had studied case law since incarceration. The court decided the Charles Vallow and Brandon Boudreaux cases would be tried separately, with the Charles Vallow case moved to March 31, 2025. Lori's trial over the murder attempt on Brandon Boudreaux was scheduled to begin in late May. On March 7, 2025, Dateline NBC aired Lori's first media interview, during which she maintained her innocence, tried to blame J.J.'s death on Tylee, claimed Jesus had shown her she and Chad would be "exonerated" and released in the future, and said she might go on Dancing with the Stars after release. In both Arizona trials, jurors were required to be unaware of Lori's prior convictions. Lori's trial over Charles' death began on March 31 with jury selection, during which she told jurors their role was to "protect" her. On April 7, in her opening statement, Lori claimed Alex Cox shot Charles in self-defense and announced she would provide proof, using the phrase "The evidence will show..." over 70 times. The prosecution argued Lori conspired to murder Charles to access his life insurance and marry Chad, that Cox staged the home to make it appear Charles attacked them, and that there was no evidence Cox was hit with a baseball bat. Lori subpoenaed several witnesses, two of whom were stricken by the court and others could not be located or served. She aggressively cross-examined a woman who had dated Charles the day before he was killed, asking if she had gone on dates with married men. Adam Cox, Lori's surviving brother, testified for the prosecution, stating he had "no doubt" Lori conspired with Alex to murder Charles, and that he and Adam had planned to confront Lori about her beliefs when Charles was killed. Kay Woodcock testified that Charles had been concerned for his safety, and evidence showed Charles was lying on the floor when he was shot the second time. Lori did not call any witnesses or testify in her own defense and made a verbal motion for a Rule 20 Judgment of Acquittal, claiming no evidence supported guilt; the judge denied it. In her closing argument, she reiterated Charles was killed in self-defense and told jurors: "Don’t let them turn my family tragedy into a crime." On April 22, 2025, Lori was found guilty of conspiring to murder Charles. After the verdict, she agreed to several aggravating factors. One juror said Lori hadn't helped her case by representing herself, noting she often smiled and laughed without taking things seriously; Kay Woodcock told reporters: "We gotcha, and you're not the smartest person in the room. Everybody's going to forget about you." On May 1, Lori filed a motion for a new trial, claiming a juror knew of her prior convictions, discovery violations, prosecutorial misconduct, lack of impartiality, and violation of the Religious Freedom Restoration Act; the motion was denied on May 23. After being found guilty of conspiring to murder Charles, Maricopa County Attorney Rachel Mitchell confirmed she intended to prosecute Lori for the murder attempt on Brandon Boudreaux, as it was important for Boudreaux to have his story vindicated. Lori filed a motion to cancel her trial over the Brandon Boudreaux case, claiming a violation of her constitutional right to a speedy trial; the judge rejected it on May 9. During the hearing, Lori argued with Judge Beresky over jury selection and witnesses. After her motion was denied, she demanded the judge recuse himself, claiming bias and religious discrimination; the judge stated he would grant a motion only if it had legal merit. On May 28, Lori filed a motion for recusal alleging "personal bias or prejudice" and religious discrimination; it was denied the next day. She filed three motions for recusal against Judge Beresky. Lori's second Arizona trial, her third and final, began on May 29 with jury selection. The next day, jury selection was halted after Lori claimed she was feeling sick. On June 2, Lori appeared in court in a wheelchair, stating she had nausea, chills, and a headache and cried loudly; the trial was postponed two days. On June 4, Lori appeared again without a wheelchair, insisting she was still sick; the judge ruled after an examination that she had no medical condition preventing her appearance and the trial proceeded. In her opening statement on June 5, Lori claimed innocence, disputed that a shooting occurred, and defined "conspiracy" by comparing her case to Judas and Cain, stating she had no malice and was "all about spreading love." Brandon Boudreaux testified about Lori's role in the breakdown of his marriage and the moment he was shot. Prosecutor Treena Kay presented evidence, including cellphone location data, showing Lori's involvement in the murder preparations. On June 6, Lori cross-examined Boudreaux and the private investigator he hired; she cast suspicion on her niece Melani by asking if she gained financially from Boudreaux's death, and the prosecutor noted Melani was under investigation. Of the few people who knew Boudreaux's new address in Gilbert, only his estranged wife had connections with Lori and Alex Cox. On June 6, Lori was briefly removed from the courtroom for failing to follow court instructions and disregarding objections; the judge threatened to revoke her self-representation. On June 9, Lori filed motions to recuse Chief Judge Jennifer Green, who had denied her motions to recuse Judge Beresky, and to "dismiss abuse of discretion"; both were denied. The Jeep's rear tire had been removed to allow the shooter to aim at Boudreaux; prosecutors showed video footage of Lori, Alex, and Chad placing a tire into a storage locker Lori rented in Rexburg. Lori did not testify or call witnesses and instead challenged nearly every piece of evidence, suggesting data could have been tampered with. In a tearful closing argument, she claimed there was no evidence against her, that she was a victim of a vendetta by Boudreaux who blamed her for the failure of his marriage and had worked for six years with law enforcement to get to her, and that healing was needed. The prosecution presented evidence of a conspiracy between Lori, Chad, Alex, and Melani. Lori again requested an acquittal outside the jury's presence, claiming the evidence was insufficient; the judge ruled against her, finding the prosecution had presented a compelling case. On June 12, Lori was found guilty of conspiring to murder Brandon Boudreaux, after the jury deliberated for less than 30 minutes. Brandon Boudreaux, standing with Kay Woodcock and Colby Ryan, stated that though facing Lori was difficult, he owed it to Charles, Tylee, J.J., and Tammy to speak, "because [he] could." On June 25, Lori filed a motion for a new trial, citing her health during the trial and lack of impartiality by the court. On June 26, she granted an interview to East Idaho News, saying she still loved Chad, reaffirmed her innocence, and predicted she and Chad would be exonerated. Her motion for a new trial was denied on July 22. Prosecutors requested a life sentence without parole for each Arizona case, to run concurrently with the Idaho convictions. Sentencing for both cases occurred on July 25. During her final testimony, Lori claimed she had been denied a fair trial and said God would set prisoners free. Judge Beresky stated Lori had "shown blatant disregard for humanity" and should never be released. Lori was given two consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole before 25 years, fined $267,000 on each case, and given a lifetime no-contact order for Brandon Boudreaux, Kay Woodcock, and several other relatives of Charles Vallow. In August, Lori filed a notice of appeal for both Arizona convictions. That same month, she was extradited back to Idaho to serve her sentences, being incarcerated at Pocatello Women's Correctional Center. In 2020, Investigation Discovery released a three-episode documentary series entitled Doomsday: The Missing Children, featuring first-hand accounts from J.J.'s grandparents Larry and Kay Woodcock, Lori's brother Adam Cox, and former KPHO-TV reporter Kim Powell. In 2021, Lifetime released a made-for-TV film titled Doomsday Mom, also marketed as The Lori Vallow Story, starring Lauren Lee Smith as Lori, Marc Blucas as Chad, Linda Purl as Kay, and Patrick Duffy as Larry. In 2022, Netflix released a three-episode documentary series entitled Sins of Our Mother, primarily from the perspective of her surviving child and Tylee's older brother, Colby Ryan. The case was also covered in investigative journalist Leah Sottile's 2022 book When the Moon Turns to Blood.
